knowledge_type_note: Unusually well evidenced for practical advice: the claims here come from large-sample studies of real games rather than from received wisdom.

history.notes: A research literature rather than a tradition; the findings here are from 2007-2026 and several are recent enough that replication is thin.

competing_claims.claim: faster decisions are associated with HIGHER quality even controlling for complexity
competing_claims.note: A separate study reports this, which sits awkwardly beside the time-pressure findings and is recorded rather than reconciled.

engine_era_note: This whole literature exists because engines made move quality measurable. Every study cited here scores human moves against an engine benchmark, which is what turned clock advice from anecdote into measurement.

preconditions: A game played with a clock
false_positive_traps: This is advice to a player about a clock, not an observation about a position, and must never be attached to a move as an explanation of it.
The evidence is about populations. It does not establish what any individual should do on any given move.
One study in this set reports faster decisions correlating with HIGHER quality, which does not obviously sit with the time-pressure findings. Both are recorded; neither is presented as settled.

typical_plans: Move quickly in the opening and in simplified endings
Spend the time in the middlegame, where the options genuinely multiply
Spend most where the position is unclear, since that is where errors compound
In severe time trouble prefer a fast move to a good slow one
strategic_consequences: Varying the spend matters more than the average spend; flexibility is the measured hallmark of strength

exceptions: A forced sequence needs no time regardless of phase.
An endgame that is theoretically critical deserves time even though endgames are generally played fast.
limitations: The studies measure populations of games, not individual decisions.
Several results are recent and thinly replicated; the blitz error-amplification study is from 2026.
This system cannot see a clock and can give no advice about one.
misconceptions: That strong players think longer. They think longer in the middlegame and shorter elsewhere, and vary more.
That mastery is intuition and time pressure therefore costs experts little. Grandmasters and world champions show strong adverse effects.
That time trouble simply makes you play worse. It makes you play worse SPECIFICALLY where the position is also unclear, and the two combine nonlinearly.

by_level.beginner: Play the opening quickly and think in the middlegame, where the position gets complicated.
by_level.intermediate: Strong players spend less time than weak ones on openings and endings and more on middlegames — and vary their spend far more.
by_level.advanced: Spend where the position is unclear: blunders rise nonlinearly when low time and an ambiguous position coincide.
by_level.master: In severe time trouble the clock becomes material — at 20 to 30 seconds in a blitz game, eight seconds was worth about a knight.

by_depth.short: Think in the middlegame; move fast elsewhere.
by_depth.normal: How to spend the clock, with unusually good evidence behind it. Across 91,000 games, strong players spend LESS time than weak players on openings and endings and significantly more on middlegames, and vary their spend far more — flexibility rather than sheer thinking time is the measured hallmark.
by_depth.deep: One of the few practical areas with real evidence. Everyone plays openings and endings faster than middlegames, and strong players exaggerate the pattern while varying their spend much more widely. The middlegame genuinely is harder - the number of reasonable options grows roughly linearly for twenty moves - but complexity stays high into the endgame while players speed up anyway, so the late speed-up is a chosen trade-off rather than a response to simplicity. Under real time pressure the clock becomes material: at 20 to 30 seconds in a three-minute game, eight seconds was worth about an extra knight. And time pressure degrades even world champions, who remain dependent on deliberation and are simply strategic about when to spend it.

explanations.hedge: These are findings about populations of games, measured against engine benchmarks; they do not determine what any individual should do on a particular move, and one study in the set points the other way.
explanations.lesson: Spend your time where the position is genuinely unclear. That is where errors multiply rather than add.

beginner_words: don't use all your time early

definition_short: How to spend the clock — and the finding that strong players spend it very differently from weak ones.
definition_long:
One of the few practical areas where there is real evidence rather than folklore.

WHERE THE TIME ACTUALLY GOES. An analysis of over 91,000 games found that everyone plays openings and endgames faster than middlegames — but that STRONG PLAYERS EXAGGERATE THE PATTERN. Players rated above 1900 spend even less time than weak players on the opening and the ending, and significantly more on middlegame moves. Their time distribution is also wider: the hallmark is not spending more time but VARYING it more, matching the spend to the position.

WHY THE MIDDLEGAME COSTS MOST is measurable. The number of reasonable options grows roughly linearly over the first twenty moves, so decisions genuinely get harder. But the same study found complexity stays high into the endgame while players speed up anyway — so the late speed-up is a deliberate shift in the speed-accuracy trade-off, not a response to a simpler position.

TIME BECOMES MATERIAL. The most striking single result: as the clock runs down, the factor determining the outcome shifts from position to time. In three-minute games with 20-30 seconds left, an eight-second advantage on the clock was worth about as much as an extra knight. Under real time pressure a fast move beats a good move that costs time.

TIME PRESSURE DEGRADES EVERYONE, including the very best. A study of twenty grandmasters and seven world champions found strong adverse effects on both speed and blunder rate, and concluded that elite players remain dependent on DELIBERATION — they are simply strategic about when to spend it. That cuts against the popular idea that mastery is mostly intuition. Consistent with it, once players are forced to play fast their normal-time rating becomes markedly less predictive of results, an effect strong at blitz and weak at rapid.

AND ERRORS CLUSTER RATHER THAN SCATTER. In a study of nearly 40,000 blitz positions, blunder probability rose NONLINEARLY when low time and an unclear position coincided — the combination is worse than the sum of its parts. The practical reading is that the moment to spend time is when the position is genuinely unclear, and the moment to move fast is when it is not.
